turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Residents told us they wanted to repair household items but didn't own equipment they might use only once. Some could afford the tools, but considered the purchase wasteful; others had nowhere to store them. We first imagined a simple shelf of donated tools. Safety advice changed our thinking: every item needed inspection, clear instructions and a reliable record of previous use. Donated equipment sometimes arrived without guards, manuals or even a clear model number, so a volunteer could not responsibly approve it just because it appeared to work. We began with forty new or professionally checked items rather than accepting everything people offered. The most popular objects aren't the electric drills, as we predicted, but basic carpet cleaners and long ladders. Booking patterns show that these are often reserved for a specific weekend task and returned immediately afterwards. That tells us the service is helping with occasional practical jobs, not replacing equipment used by professionals. Anyone with a library card can borrow most tools after watching a ten-minute safety video. Cutting equipment requires an additional in-person demonstration. Items are normally lent for four days. We considered a deposit, but that could exclude people the project is intended to help, so late returns are handled by temporarily suspending further borrowing. Someone who contacts us before the deadline may receive an extension if nobody else has booked the item. Next spring we hope to run repair workshops. These won't be classes where an expert fixes things for you; participants will bring an object and learn alongside volunteers how to diagnose the problem. The aim is to make the reasoning visible, including the decision to stop when a repair requires professional knowledge. Our biggest challenge now is storage. Demand justifies expanding the collection, but there is little unused space in the present building.
